statement: In the world's population, alcohol use compared with no alcohol use is estimated by two global models to account for about 2.3 million (2004, after subtracting deaths the model counted as prevented; editors' rounding) to 2.8 million (2016) deaths a year. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016 (95% uncertainty interval 2.4–3.3 million), 2.2% of age-standardised deaths in women and 6.8% in men, about 2 and 7 in every 100; it ranked alcohol seventh among risk factors overall and first at ages 15 to 49, where 3.8% of women's and 12.2% of men's deaths were attributed to it, the leading causes being tuberculosis, road injuries and self-harm (Griswold et al., 2018; funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation). A WHO comparative risk assessment for 2004 estimated 2482 thousand deaths caused by alcohol, less 227 thousand deaths it modelled as prevented (215 thousand from heart and blood-vessel disease, 12 thousand from diabetes), leaving 2255 thousand, 3.8 in every 100 deaths worldwide (6.3 in 100 deaths of men and 1.1 in 100 of women) and 5.3 in 100 deaths before the age of 60; the deaths caused were mainly from unintentional injuries (666 thousand), heart and blood-vessel disease (545 thousand), cancer (487 thousand), liver cirrhosis (373 thousand) and intentional injuries (272 thousand) (Rehm et al., 2009; the underlying assessments supported by WHO and the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health; no conflicts declared). These are model estimates, not counted deaths: they combine estimated drinking (sales data, estimates of unrecorded alcohol, which is more than a quarter of the world's drinking, and surveys) with relative-risk curves from observational studies, mostly of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries, applied to every population. The 2004 estimate has no uncertainty intervals, and the 2016 paper does not say that its intervals include uncertainty from the model's structure or from bias in the underlying studies; the net figures depend on protective heart and diabetes estimates at low intake, which the 2004 authors call controversial; the 2016 figure is counted against a minimum-risk level of zero drinks a day, whose interval reached 0.8 drinks (10 g each) a day and which moved to about half a drink a day when the same group updated its weights (0.534, 0–1.00; Bryazka et al., 2022); the 2016 authors expect their figures to be underestimates, because drinking patterns, harm to others from violence and people under 15 were left out; and the two estimates used different methods and inputs, so the difference between them is not a trend. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: Two global models estimated that alcohol caused about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, compared with no one drinking. The Global Burden of Disease study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016: about 7 in 100 deaths of men and 2 in 100 of women. At ages 15 to 49, alcohol was the top risk factor in that study (about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women), the leading causes being tuberculosis, road injuries and self-harm. An older WHO model estimated about 2.5 million deaths caused in 2004, minus about 0.2 million it counted as prevented, mainly from heart disease; that is about 4 in 100 of all deaths. Injuries, heart and blood-vessel disease, cancer and liver cirrhosis made up most of the deaths caused. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths. They rely on studies of groups of people, mostly in richer countries, and the two models used different methods, so the numbers cannot be compared as a trend.
population: The world's population: all ages in the 2004 WHO comparative risk assessment (14 WHO subregions); ages 15 and over in the Global Burden of Disease 2016 study (195 locations)
exposure: Alcohol use as modelled from sales data (recorded and unrecorded alcohol) and surveys: average volume, with drinking patterns for injuries and ischaemic heart disease, in the 2004 model; average grams of ethanol a day among current drinkers (10-g standard drinks) in the 2016 model
comparator: A counterfactual of no alcohol use (2004), or the estimated minimum-risk level of zero drinks a day (2016)
outcome: Deaths attributable to alcohol: in 2004, deaths caused, deaths prevented and net deaths (WHO Global Burden of Disease 2004 causes); in 2016, attributable deaths from 23 outcomes
magnitude: Griswold et al. 2018 (GBD 2016; 95% uncertainty intervals): 2.8 million (2.4–3.3) deaths in 2016; 2.2% (1.5–3.0) of age-standardised female and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4–2.0) and 6.0% (5.4–6.7) of DALYs; ages 15–49: 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths; leading attributable causes at 15–49: tuberculosis 1.4% (1.0–1.7), road injuries 1.2% (0.7–1.9) and self-harm 1.1% (0.6–1.5) of total deaths; minimum-risk level 0 (0.0–0.8) standard drinks of 10 g a day. Rehm et al. 2009 (WHO comparative risk assessment, 2004; thousands; no intervals): caused 2482 (men 2039, women 443); prevented 227 (cardiovascular 215, diabetes 12); net 2255 (men 1944, women 311) of 58 738 deaths, 3.8% (men 6.3%, women 1.1%); under age 60, 5.3% (men 7.9%, women 1.9%); deaths caused by cause: unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric 135, perinatal 3. Bryazka et al. 2022: global minimum-risk level 0.534 (0–1.00) drinks a day with the GBD 2016 curves and GBD 2020 weights.

evidence.extracted: Alcohol-attributable deaths in 2004, in thousands rounded to the nearest thousand, against no alcohol consumption: caused 2482 (men 2039, women 443), of which unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular diseases 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis of the liver 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric disorders 135 and maternal and perinatal disorders 3; prevented 227 (cardiovascular diseases 215, diabetes 12); net 2255 (men 1944, women 311) of 58 738 deaths in all (men 31 063, women 27 674), that is 3.8% of all deaths (men 6.3%, women 1.1%), against 3.2% in the comparative risk assessment for 2000. Editors' calculation: deaths caused are 4.2% of all deaths, and injuries, cardiovascular disease, cancer and cirrhosis make up 2343 of the 2482 thousand.

3.8% of deaths at all ages and 5.3% of deaths in people younger than 60 years were attributable to alcohol (7.9% in men, 1.9% in women), mainly through injuries, with most beneficial effects in older age groups.

evidence.locator: Alcohol as a risk factor for disease, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors describe the reduced incidence of ischaemic cardiovascular outcomes and diabetes linked to regular drinking at low amounts as controversial, and estimate these beneficial effects anyway, together with the net burden.

Alcohol-attributable fractions combine the prevalence of each exposure category with its relative risk against no consumption, from meta-analyses; the fractions for chronic diseases were taken from the comparative risk assessment for 2002 and those for injuries from that for 2000, and take account of drinking patterns for ischaemic heart disease and injuries; the counterfactual of no alcohol consumption is the same for harmful and beneficial effects.

Limitations stated: more than 25% of global consumption is estimated to be unrecorded, mainly from expert opinion; drinking patterns were estimated from nearby countries or expert opinion; relative risks from meta-analyses based predominantly on middle-class cohorts in developed countries were assumed to transfer to every country; alcohol-attributable infectious diseases were not included; the uncertainty is described as fairly low compared with other risk factors, citing an earlier WHO report. No uncertainty intervals are given for the burden estimates (editors' observation).

Global, age-standardised, both-sexes minimum-risk level (TMREL): GBD 2016 as published 0 (0–0.800); GBD 2016 curves with GBD 2020 DALY weights 0.534 (0–1.00); GBD 2020 curves and weights 0.511 (0.400–0.700) standard drinks a day.

risk_of_bias.note: The estimates take as causal and unbiased the relative-risk curves fitted to observational studies (592 studies in the 2016 model, with no quality appraisal described in the main text; meta-analyses mainly of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries in 2004); the protective low-intake curves for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes, which subtract 227 thousand deaths in 2004, are where confounding and abstainer bias are most disputed (cards sc_griswold_2018 and sc_rehm_2009, editors' checklist overall high).

inconsistency.note: The two models give figures of similar size (2.3 to 2.8 million a year) for different years and with different methods.

indirectness.note: Relative risks transferred to every population; exposure from sales data, expert estimates of unrecorded alcohol (more than a quarter of the total) and surveys; drinking patterns estimated from nearby countries or expert opinion in 2004; harm to others only through US road-injury data in 2016; the 2016 counterfactual from one global weighting of the curves.

imprecision.note: No uncertainty intervals in the 2004 model; the 2016 intervals (2.4 to 3.3 million) are not said to include structural uncertainty or bias in the underlying studies.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a model; publication bias in the studies behind the curves is covered under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Model estimates are not graded as evidence of an effect: the claim describes what the models estimate (relation describes), and its certainty comes from the observational evidence behind the relative-risk curves (low), rated down for the models' indirectness and their incomplete uncertainty, which gives very low. No upgrade applies to a modelled count. Status replicated by the same team: the two estimates come from different groups but share the comparative-risk-assessment method, much of the underlying literature and WHO exposure data, so their agreement is not independent replication (METHODS §6.3); the flag's definition covers a shared analysis model.
